Chicago by the numbers

Who assesses and bills property tax in Chicago?

Chicago sits in Cook County, so two county offices run the system for the city. The Cook County Assessor values the property, and the Cook County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. A third body, the Cook County Board of Review, hears appeals once the Assessor has finished its pass.

  • Assessor's Office: sets estimated market values, mails reassessment notices and accepts first-level appeals when a township opens.
  • Board of Review: a separate appeal level with its own township calendar.
  • Treasurer's Office: sends the bills, takes payments and runs the delinquent tax sale. It is at 118 North Clark Street, Room 212, Chicago, IL 60602.

The Treasurer's site lets an owner get a copy of a bill, search for delinquent taxes on a property, view the taxing district debt attributed to it and search for missing senior exemptions.

What makes Chicago different from other Illinois places for a seller?

Chicago is far larger and more varied than any other Illinois place. It had an estimated 2,731,585 residents by mid-2025, packed into 227.73 square miles on the western shore of Lake Michigan. It was incorporated as a city in 1837, and the Great Chicago Fire of October 8, 1871 destroyed a large section and left more than 100,000 people homeless.

Sociologists subdivided the city into 75 community areas in the late 1920s, and O'Hare in 1956 and Edgewater in 1980 brought the total to 77. Those areas hold more than 200 informal neighborhoods. Away from the lake, large stretches of the residential map are brick bungalows built from the early twentieth century through World War II, mixed with two-flats, townhouses, condominiums and apartment buildings. A bungalow in one area and a condo near the Loop can have bills that look unrelated.

Transit matters to value. The Chicago L, Metra and Pace buses together carry about 1.3 million rides a day, and O'Hare was ranked the busiest airport in the world by takeoffs and landings in 2025. Winters are cold and snowy, with measurable snow possible into early April, and summer highs can top 90 degrees on about 17 days.

What do Census numbers say about Chicago housing?

Owners live in 46.0% of Chicago's occupied homes, so renters are the majority. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures are below.

Chicago city, Census QuickFacts
MeasureChicago
Estimated residents, mid-20252,731,585
Owner-occupied housing unit rate46.0%
Typical owner-occupied home value$334,100
Median gross rent$1,440
Households1,160,205
Median household income$77,902
Mean travel time to work, minutes33.1
Foreign-born persons20.9%

Those are citywide medians. The Treasurer's analysis found that residential values in Chicago moved from a median decrease of 7.7% to an increase of 131.8% depending on the area, so the figure for your own street can sit far from the table.

When are Chicago property tax installments due?

Cook County dates move from year to year, and the Treasurer posts each one. The 2025 tax year first installment was due Wednesday, April 1, 2026, and the second was due Thursday, October 1, 2026. Both dates have passed.

Earlier years show how much the calendar shifts:

  • Tax year 2025: April 1, 2026 and October 1, 2026.
  • Tax year 2024: March 4, 2025 and December 15, 2025.
  • Tax year 2023: March 1, 2024 and August 1, 2024.

Read the dates printed on your own bill, and check the Treasurer's due-dates page before any payment.

Exemptions appear as deductions on the second installment bill, according to the Assessor's site, which matters if you are a seller waiting on a credit. If a Certificate of Error for a valuation correction has been approved, refund timing comes from the Treasurer's Office.

How do Chicago assessment appeals work?

Cook County uses a two-level appeal system, and each level opens township by township. Chicago is divided into several townships, and the Assessor's 2026 calendar for the city lists last file dates by township. Rogers Park closed June 1, Lakeview July 13, Hyde Park October 8, Lake October 29 and Jefferson November 12. North Chicago's last file date was November 24, and South Chicago's was December 15.

Chicago was not being reassessed in 2026, though a property could still be revalued after division work, permits or other special circumstances, and its owner would then receive a reassessment notice. Properties in Cook County are reassessed on a three-year cycle, with the city, the north suburbs and the south and west suburbs rotating. The Board of Review runs its own township dates, and the Assessor's calendar lists Board of Review windows such as August 3 to September 1, 2026 for Rogers Park, and August 31 to September 29 for Lakeview.

The Board of Review publishes a Township and Exemption Dates document each year, and it is the place to confirm your township's window.

What do Chicago owners actually pay?

The Treasurer's 2025 tax year analysis says the median Chicago homeowner bill rose 3.2% to $4,597. Overall Chicago taxes rose $196 million, or 2.2%, below the 3.1% rate of inflation for 2025, and homeowners picked up about three-fifths of that increase. Nearly 660,000 residential properties saw higher taxes, while fewer than 66,000 saw lower ones.

Countywide, the same report counts nearly 1.8 million bills for the 2025 tax year and a total levy above $19.9 billion. Commercial values in Chicago continued to decline, which shifts more of the load onto homes.

Exemptions soften it. The Homeowner Exemption reduces a home's equalized assessed value by $10,000, applies to single-family homes, townhouses, condominiums, co-ops and buildings up to six units, and is renewed automatically for properties that were not sold in the last year. New owners must apply. Additional senior, senior freeze, disability and military exemptions are listed on the Treasurer's site.

What happens to unpaid Chicago property tax?

The Treasurer's site lists a delinquent tax sale for December 15, 2026, with brochures on how to avoid it in English, Spanish and Polish. Taxes for tax year 2023 are the ones on the lists of properties with delinquent taxes. The Treasurer also keeps a page titled If Taxes Were Sold for owners whose taxes have already gone to sale.

Search a PIN on the Treasurer's site to see whether any tax is delinquent. A seller with a delinquent year should ask the Treasurer and the title company for the payoff figure before closing.

What transfer tax applies when you sell in Chicago?

The City of Chicago's Real Property Transfer Tax is $5.25 per $500 of the transfer price, or fraction thereof. The Department of Finance's page says that, in general, the buyer is responsible for $3.75 and the seller for $1.50, and the $1.50 is the supplemental portion for the Chicago Transit Authority.

The exemptions page lists transfers to or from a governmental body, deeds that secure debt, transfers under $500 and tax deeds. A refund of the CTA portion exists for buyers 65 or older who occupy the home for at least a year, when the price is $250,000 or less. The Tax Division is at 2 N. La Salle Street, Suite 1310. The Illinois state tax of 50 cents per $500 under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is a separate tax.

More questions about Chicago, IL Property Tax Guide

Who bills property tax in Chicago?

The Cook County Treasurer's Office. The Cook County Assessor sets the values, and the Board of Review hears appeals.

When was the second installment of the 2025 tax year due in Chicago?

Thursday, October 1, 2026. The first installment was due Wednesday, April 1, 2026.

What is the Cook County Homeowner Exemption?

A $10,000 reduction in a home's equalized assessed value for owner-occupied residences of up to six units. It appears on the second installment bill, and new owners must apply.

How much is the Chicago transfer tax?

$5.25 per $500 of transfer price. The Department of Finance says the buyer generally owes $3.75 and the seller $1.50.

Is there a Cook County tax sale in December 2026?

The Treasurer's site lists a delinquent tax sale on December 15, 2026 and publishes guides on avoiding it.

Champaign by the numbers

Which county offices bill property tax for the city of Champaign?

The city of Champaign does not send its own property tax bill. The Champaign County Treasurer, who also acts as Collector, bills every parcel in the city along with the school districts and other taxing districts that share it. Valuation sits with the Champaign County Supervisor of Assessments, and the city is coterminous with Champaign City township, so one township assessor covers the whole municipality.

That arrangement keeps the paperwork simple for a seller. One PIN identifies the parcel, and the same two county offices answer questions whether the house is near Campustown, downtown or on the northwest side near Parkland College.

What is the city of Champaign like for a home seller?

Champaign is a council-manager city of about 23 square miles on high, flat ground in central Illinois, founded in 1855 as West Urbana when the Illinois Central Railroad ran its tracks two miles west of Urbana's downtown. It took the Champaign name when it received a city charter in 1860. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign sits on the east side and Parkland College on the northwest, which gives the market a large student population during the school year.

The economy leans on the university, Research Park, health care and food manufacturing. Kraft's plant is described as one of the largest pasta factories in North America, and technology firms keep offices in the park south of State Farm Center. Champaign Unit 4 School District serves the city, with Champaign Central and Centennial high schools. I-57, I-72 and I-74 meet here, and Willard Airport and the Illinois Terminal rail and bus hub sit within the area.

Weather affects older houses in practical ways. Temperatures top 90 degrees Fahrenheit on about 24 days a year and drop below 0 on about six nights, and the winters are moderately snowy. Roofs and heating systems are the usual items to look at before listing a house built in the 1980s or earlier.

How does Champaign compare with the county in Census numbers?

Renters are the majority in the city, which is the main difference from the rest of Champaign County. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates put the owner-occupied rate at 43.8% in the city and 54.0% across the county.

Champaign city and Champaign County, Census QuickFacts
MeasureChampaign cityChampaign County
Estimated residents, mid-202591,195209,972
Land area, 2020, square miles22.93996.10
Owner-occupied rate43.8%54.0%
Typical owner-occupied home value$210,900$211,500
Median gross rent$1,123$1,051
Median household income$56,118$63,683
Mean travel time to work, minutes14.916.9

The city's median home value sits close to the countywide figure, while its rents run higher. A landlord selling a rental near campus will often deal with tenants and a lease cycle, and the tax bill follows the parcel regardless of who lives in it.

When is Champaign property tax due?

Bills are mailed by early May and fall due in two installments. The Treasurer's FAQ gives June 3 and September 3 for the 2025 tax year, and a payment postmarked on the due date is on time. Each coupon carries its own dates, so use the bill in front of you for any later year.

Interest of 1.5% a month applies to late payments, and the Treasurer accepts personal checks through September 30. A returned payment is void and costs $30 plus statutory interest. Cards and eCheck work online or by phone at 217-834-8713, and a fee goes to the processing vendor. In person, the Treasurer's counter is at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana.

How can a Champaign owner challenge an assessment?

The Board of Review takes complaints from July 1 through September 10. Its hours are 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday, or by appointment. Township assessors value a home on January 1 at one-third of market value, and owners receive change notices from the Supervisor of Assessments before the complaint window opens.

Gather evidence that fits the property. For a house, that means your purchase price if you bought recently, a recent appraisal, and sales of similar homes in the same neighborhood. After September 10 the board reviews the complaints and issues written decisions.

Which parts of Champaign shape the housing market?

Several districts pull demand in different directions, and a buyer's questions change with the street. The ones that stand out in the city's history and layout are these:

  • Downtown Champaign: the historic core around the Virginia Theatre and the City Building, with newer mixed-use buildings and a parking deck added during a revitalization effort.
  • Campustown: the Green Street district beside the university, where high-rise student apartments have opened since 2008.
  • North Prospect: a shopping corridor on the city's northern edge that grew out into former farmland.
  • Northwest and west sides: home to Parkland College and the private St. Thomas More High School.

The city has 60 parks and 11 trails, and the Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District runs buses across Champaign, Urbana and Savoy. Those details help a listing for a family house, while investors selling near campus tend to talk about the rental cycle instead.

Which exemptions can a Champaign homeowner claim?

The Assessment Office lists several homestead reductions, each applied to equalized assessed value before the rate is multiplied:

  • General homestead, $6,000, for a primary residence on January 1.
  • Senior citizens, $5,000, for owners who turn 65 by year end.
  • Senior assessment freeze, with a maximum household income of $75,000, renewed each year.
  • Persons with disabilities, $2,000.
  • Disabled veterans, scaled by disability rating.
  • Returning veterans, $5,000 for two years.

For forms, call the Assessment Office at 217-384-3760. The office cannot accept faxed or emailed applications. Owners who moved in recently should ask whether an earlier owner's exemption carried over before assuming it did.

What happens if Champaign property tax is not paid?

Unpaid tax is sold to a buyer at the county's annual sale, which the Treasurer's FAQ places on October 30 for amounts still open after 4:30 p.m. on October 29. The house is not sold. After the sale the owner owes the amount sold plus interest and redeems through the County Clerk at 217-384-3722.

The Clerk sends a Take Notice within four months of the sale. State law, in 35 ILCS 200/21-350, sets a redemption period that is generally 3 years from the date of sale, subject to listed exceptions. If the owner does not redeem in time, the buyer may petition the circuit court for a deed.

How do you sell a Champaign house when tax is still due?

Start with the PIN. Ask the Treasurer which installments are paid, and read the closing documents or ask the title company or attorney whether tax is owed for the year. The Treasurer notes that, depending on the closing and recording dates, a bill may be addressed to the previous owner, who must forward it to the new owner.

If installments are open, ask the title company how they will be handled at closing. Knowing the number early gives you room to plan the closing date. For a rental in the city, add the tenants' lease end date to the same checklist.

More questions about Champaign, IL Property Tax Guide

Does the city of Champaign collect its own property tax?

No. The Champaign County Treasurer bills and collects all property tax for parcels in the city, then distributes it to the taxing districts.

What are the 2025 tax year due dates in Champaign?

June 3 for the first installment and September 3 for the second, according to the Treasurer's FAQ. A payment postmarked on the due date counts as on time.

When can I file an assessment complaint for a Champaign home?

Between July 1 and September 10, with the Champaign County Board of Review, which is open 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Thursday.

What is the senior exemption in Champaign?

A $5,000 reduction in equalized assessed value for owners who reach 65 by the end of the assessment year. A separate freeze applies up to a $75,000 household income.

Is the owner-occupied rate in Champaign higher than the county's?

No. The Census Bureau shows 43.8% owner-occupied in the city and 54.0% across Champaign County for 2020 to 2024.

Bloomington by the numbers

Who bills property tax on a Bloomington house?

McLean County bills it. Bloomington is the county seat, and the county treasurer and tax collector sends one bill per parcel on behalf of nearly 200 taxing districts, covering about 68,000 parcels. That office works from the Government Center, 115 E. Washington Street, Room M101, and answers at (309) 888-5180.

Assessment is a separate job. The City of Bloomington Township assessor values property inside the city, the county Supervisor of Assessments (the chief county assessment officer) handles equalization and exemptions at (309) 888-5130, and the county Board of Review hears complaints. The city government itself does not send a property tax bill, though it registers rental buildings and collects its own local taxes.

  • County treasurer: payments, duplicate bills, delinquent tax and the annual tax sale.
  • Township assessor and county assessor: values, property record cards, exemptions and address changes.
  • Board of Review: assessment complaints, reached at (309) 888-5132.

What is Bloomington like for someone selling a home?

The 2020 census counted 78,680 people, placing Bloomington 13th among Illinois cities and fifth outside the Chicago area. It sits beside Normal, and the pair anchor a metro of roughly 170,000 people. The town dates to 1831 and was named seat when McLean County was created. Illinois Wesleyan University, State Farm and Country Financial are major local institutions, and Beer Nuts snacks are made only here.

Interstates 39, 55 and 74 meet at Bloomington, with US 51, US 150 and Illinois Route 9 also passing through. Two public systems serve the city, Bloomington District 87 and McLean County Unit District 5, and small portions reach into Olympia District 16. Weather runs from a January average low near 14 degrees to a July high near 86.

  • The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 78,804 residents, a 0.1% rise since 2020.
  • Owners live in 61.9% of occupied homes, so roughly 38 in 100 are rented, which matters if you sell to an investor.
  • Typical owned homes are valued at $203,300, and renters pay a median of $1,050 a month.
  • Median household income of $77,384 and a 16.8-minute average commute.

When are McLean County tax bills due?

McLean County's treasurer states that taxes are always due in the first week of June and the first week of September. For 2026 the dates were June 10 and September 10, and the treasurer posts that all dates are subject to change. The county says a person who never receives a bill is still liable under 35 ILCS 200/20-15, and asks owners without a bill by mid-May to call for a duplicate.

McLean County 2026 collection calendar for tax year 2025 (source: McLean County Treasurer)
DateEvent
May 7Real estate bills scheduled to be mailed
June 10First installment due
September 10Second installment due
October 9Last day to pay in the office by personal check
October 12$10.00 certified fee and delinquency letters
November 5Judgment hearing; last day to pay to avoid the sale
November 6Delinquent tax sale begins at 10:00 a.m.

Those 2026 dates are all in the past. Late payments carry interest of 1.5% per month, starting the day after the due date, and a payment postmarked by the due date is on time.

How do I pay a Bloomington property tax bill?

The treasurer lists several routes. Partial payments are not accepted, and no receipt is mailed unless you ask, since a canceled check or bank statement stands in as proof.

  • By mail to the lockbox: McLean County Collector, P.O. Box 843637, Kansas City, MO 64184-3637.
  • In person at 115 E. Washington Street, Monday to Friday, 8:00 until 4:30.
  • At a drop box, open around the clock, on the Washington Street side of the lot or at the East Street entrance.
  • Online or by phone with a credit card, with a convenience fee, or through annual automatic withdrawal.
  • At a participating local bank.

After October 9, the office requires certified funds for payments, and no payments are taken on the day of the sale. A mortgage company asking for a duplicate bill pays a $5.00 fee under state law. If you refinanced or paid off a mortgage, file a change of address with the Supervisor of Assessments so future bills reach you.

How can a Bloomington owner challenge an assessment?

An owner has 30 days after the township's notice appears in the newspaper to file a complaint with the Board of Review. For 2026, the City of Bloomington Township notice ran in the Pantagraph on September 29 with a filing deadline of October 29 and an equalization factor of 1.0385. Bloomington Township, a separate township in the same county, had the same dates and a factor of 1.0534. Check which township your parcel is in before you rely on either number.

The county explains that the assessment reflects the past three years of market value before January 1 of the assessment year, and an equalization factor is applied to bring the result to 33.33%. A late complaint will not be heard. Owners use form PTAX-230 for nonfarm property, and the Board meets in the Supervisor of Assessments' office in the Government Center. The Board's 2026 schedule ran from June into mid-December.

Following the severe storms of June 30, 2026, McLean County was named in a state disaster declaration, which lets owners apply for reassessment on form PTAX-245. A second declaration followed on August 18, 2026. Owners of storm-damaged homes should ask the assessor whether that process applies.

Which homestead exemptions apply in McLean County?

Exemptions reduce the taxable value before the rate is applied, so the dollar saving depends on your tax rate. Only a primary residence qualifies, and the county's own page lists these:

  • General homestead: up to $6,000, filed first with the chief county assessment officer.
  • Homestead improvement: up to $75,000 of market value, or $25,000 assessed, usually granted automatically for four years.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000, with an initial PTAX-324 and proof of age.
  • Low-income senior freeze: household income under $75,000, using PTAX-340, which the county mails each year around February 1 to current senior exemption holders.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000, renewed yearly with the county's December 31 due date.
  • Returning veterans: $5,000 for the year the veteran returns and the following year.
  • Disabled veterans: $2,500, $5,000 or up to $250,000, depending on the rating.

The senior deferral program is run through the treasurer at (309) 888-5180. A buyer must file their own claims after closing.

What rules does the city add for rental houses?

An investor selling a rental should know that the City of Bloomington requires every owner of residential rental property inside the city limits to register it each year. Its Rental Property Program prints a fee of $65 per building, plus $5 per unit in buildings with three or more units, and registrations run through December 31.

The city states that a registration cannot be transferred to a new owner, so a buyer registers again. It also states that no one may rent or occupy a covered building without a Certificate of Inspection. A building rated "fair" may need a $5,000 letter of credit or pledged account until it passes, and follow-up inspections are charged at $100 per appointment. A missed inspection costs $75. Fix any open violations before you list, since they affect a buyer's repair requests.

More questions about Bloomington, IL Property Tax Guide

Which office do I call about a Bloomington property tax bill?

Call the McLean County treasurer at (309) 888-5180 for payments and duplicate bills, and the county assessor at (309) 888-5130 for values, exemptions and mailing addresses. The city of Bloomington does not send the bill.

When is the second installment of Bloomington property tax due?

It falls in the first week of September each year. For 2026 the county listed September 10. Interest of 1.5% per month starts the day after the due date.

Did Bloomington taxpayers have a deadline to appeal in 2026?

Yes. The City of Bloomington Township filing deadline was October 29, 2026, thirty days after its September 29 notice. That date has passed, so watch for next year's newspaper notice.

Does Bloomington require rental registration when I sell?

Registration belongs to the owner, and the city says it cannot transfer to a new owner. A buyer of a rental registers anew and pays the printed fee of $65 per building.

Can I pay McLean County tax with a card?

Yes, online or by phone, with a convenience fee. The office also accepts mail, in-person payments, a 24-hour drop box, local banks and annual automatic withdrawal.

Evanston by the numbers

Who assesses and bills property tax in Evanston, Illinois?

Cook County does, not the City of Evanston. The Cook County Assessor's Office values the property, the Cook County Board of Review hears assessment appeals, and the Cook County Treasurer mails the bills and collects the money. Evanston is its own assessment township, so an Evanston parcel is grouped with other Evanston parcels when the Assessor reassesses.

The city does collect other charges tied to a sale, including the local real estate transfer tax and the final water bill, covered below. Evanston property sits in Evanston-Skokie School District 65 for grades through 8 and Evanston Township High School District 202 for high school, and those districts are two of the taxing bodies that appear on a tax bill.

When are Cook County property tax installments due for Evanston owners?

The Cook County Treasurer lists April 1, 2026 as the due date for the first installment of tax year 2025 and October 1, 2026 as the second. Both dates have passed. The dates differ from year to year, so use the ones printed on your own bill.

County officials said the 2025 second installment bills were expected to go out on September 1, 2026, about two months later than usual. They blamed a technology overhaul of the county property tax system. Property owners could view bills online before the mailing.

Mail payments follow a strict rule under Illinois law: only mail carrying a United States Postal Service postmark counts as paid on the mailing date, while FedEx or UPS deliveries count on the day they arrive. A mailed payment may be returned if it lacks the PIN or the original coupon. In person, the Treasurer takes payment at nearly 400 Chase Bank locations in Illinois and some community banks, and delinquent bills go to the Treasurer's office at 118 North Clark Street in Chicago.

How does the Cook County Assessor value an Evanston home?

Single-family homes, condos and small apartment buildings fall in Class 2, and a Class 2 property is assessed at 10% of its estimated market value. Cook County reassesses each township once every three years.

Evanston owners were mailed reassessment notices on April 9, 2025 and had until May 21, 2025 to appeal. The Assessor's figures for Evanston Township show how far its estimates sat from sales that year:

  • Single-family homes: $675,000 median sale price in 2024, $636,000 Assessor estimate for 2025
  • Condos: $294,000 median sale price in 2024, $265,000 estimate for 2025
  • Small apartment buildings: $620,000 median sale price in 2024, $592,000 estimate for 2025

The taxable figure is the equalized assessed value, which is the assessed value times a yearly equalizer that the Illinois Department of Revenue sets for all of Cook County. Exemptions then come off that number. The Homeowner Exemption subtracts $10,000 of equalized assessed value and the Senior Exemption subtracts $8,000, and both currently renew automatically.

How do I appeal an Evanston assessment?

You file with the Assessor first and then, if needed, with the Board of Review, and each only accepts filings while the township is open. Appeals to the Assessor are online and free, and no attorney is required.

The Assessor names three reasons to file:

  • Lack of uniformity, where similar nearby homes carry lower assessments
  • Overvaluation, supported by a recent closing statement or purchase prices of comparable homes
  • Incorrect description, such as wrong square footage on the notice

The office offers a rule of thumb. If the listed characteristics are right and the estimate is within 10% of what you believe the home is worth, an appeal is unlikely to change the bill much. Its 2026 calendar lists Evanston as closed, with a notice date of April 22, 2026, a last file date of June 4, 2026 and Board of Review appeals from August 3 to September 1, 2026. The Assessor also says it does not set a home's value equal to one recent sale.

If a reassessment is granted and nothing about the property changes, that value stands until the next reassessment. An owner who missed a window can appeal the next time the township opens. An approved Certificate of Error corrects a valuation after the fact, and refunds are handled by the Treasurer.

What transfer taxes apply when an Evanston house sells?

Evanston has charged its own real estate transfer tax since 1986, under Ordinance 33-O-86. The city says it is typically paid by the seller unless the contract says otherwise, and the money goes to the General Fund. State stamps add another charge, priced at 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction, per 35 ILCS 200/31-15.

City of Evanston transfer tax rates (source: City of Evanston Real Estate Transfer Tax)
Sale priceRate per $1,000 of value
Up to $1,500,000$5
$1,500,000.01 to $5,000,000$7
Over $5,000,000$9

Exempt transactions carry a $100 stamp fee under Evanston City Code 3-25-8-1. Since Ordinance 18-O-25, the city issues electronic transfer stamps.

How do I get an Evanston transfer stamp before closing?

Submit a request through the city's online service request portal or by calling the 3-1-1 center at 847-448-4311. In-person applications are not accepted.

  • Send the request 7 to 10 business days before closing
  • Allow 5 business days for processing, starting the business day after the city receives it
  • Expect no expedited handling, with no exceptions
  • Upload the signed Evanston Real Estate Declaration Form, plus the sale contract or deed, to the service request

The city issues the stamp only after documents check out and all debts owed to the city are paid. The final water bill is generated with the request, except for condos and vacant land, and is paid through the city's water billing site. Payment can be made online, in person at the City Collector's Office at 909 Davis Street, or by mail. Stamps of $5,000 to $49,999 need a credit card, cashier's check, title company check or wire, and $50,000 or more requires a cashier's check or wire.

What does the Evanston housing market look like on paper?

Evanston lies on Lake Michigan about 12 miles north of the Loop, with Chicago to the south, Skokie to the west and Wilmette to the north. Northwestern University was founded here in 1851, the community incorporated as a town in 1863, and voters organized it as a city in 1892. Land area is 7.78 square miles.

QuickFacts shows 76,380 people for 2025 and 31,705 households. Over 2020 through 2024, the median owner-occupied home was valued at $481,200, owners lived in 56.2% of housing units, and household income had a median of $96,434. Rent had a median of $1,762 and 69.5% of adults over 25 held at least a bachelor's degree.

The CTA Purple Line serves Evanston, and Metra's Union Pacific North line stops at Main Street, Davis Street and Central Street. Downtown centers on Davis Street, with shopping along Central, Dempster and Main. A 2015 state list put Northwestern University, NorthShore University HealthSystem and School District 65 at the top of the employer ranking.

How is property tax settled at an Evanston closing?

Cook County bills in two installments for a tax year that has already ended. The sale contract and the title company decide how the current bills are divided between seller and buyer.

Check which exemptions show on the current bill. The Treasurer's site offers tools to see how a bill changed, view taxing district debt and search for missing senior exemptions. A seller behind on tax should get the payoff balance from the Treasurer so the title company can clear it at closing.

More questions about Evanston, IL Property Tax Guide

Who sends the property tax bill for an Evanston house?

The Cook County Treasurer sends it, not the City of Evanston. Bills go out in two installments, and tax year 2025 installments were due April 1 and October 1, 2026. The County Assessor sets the value the bill rests on.

How much is Evanston's real estate transfer tax?

Evanston charges $5 per $1,000 of value on sales up to $1,500,000, $7 on the slice from $1,500,000.01 to $5,000,000 and $9 above that. The city says the seller usually pays unless the contract states otherwise. A $100 fee applies to exempt transfers.

How long does an Evanston transfer stamp take?

Plan on 5 business days after the city receives your request, and submit it 7 to 10 business days before closing. The city offers no expedited service and accepts requests only online or through 3-1-1.

What were the 2026 Evanston appeal dates?

The Assessor's last file date for Evanston was June 4, 2026, after notices dated April 22, 2026. Board of Review appeals ran August 3 through September 1, 2026. Owners can appeal again when the township next opens.

What percent of market value is an Evanston home assessed at?

Class 2 residential property in Cook County is assessed at 10% of estimated market value. Taxes then use the equalized assessed value, which multiplies the assessed value by the state equalizer and subtracts exemptions such as the $10,000 Homeowner Exemption.
